name: Sermorelin

b.x: Twenty-nine amino acids. That's what separates the sermorelin peptide (also known as Geref or GRF 1-29) from the full 44-amino-acid endogenous GHRH molecule, and those 29 amino acids are the only ones that matter for receptor binding. Sermorelin acetate (CAS 86168-78-7) is a synthetic analog of human GHRH(1-29)NH2 that retains complete GHRH receptor affinity on pituitary somatotroph cells. The mechanism is direct. Sermorelin binds the GHRH receptor, triggering pulsatile GH release that mirrors the body's natural secretion pattern. Unlike exogenous growth hormone injections, this preserves the hypothalamic-pituitary feedback loop. The pituitary decides how much GH to release; sermorelin just gives it a stronger signal to do so. That distinction matters for long-term safety. Khorram and colleagues gave 19 adults aged 55 to 71 a nightly GHRH analog, [Nle27]GHRH(1-29)-NH2 [1]. Treatment ran 16 weeks after a 4-week placebo run-in. IGF-1 rose within two weeks, then drifted back toward baseline by week 16. Skin thickness rose, and lean mass increased in men only; sleep quality and fat mass didn't change. The Geref International Study Group [2] treated 110 GH-deficient children with 30 mcg/kg/day for up to a year. Height velocity in the 86 children analyzed rose from 4.1 to 7.2 cm per year at 12 months. A later review [4] notes that data in a few children suggest the effect holds through 36 months. Subcutaneous bioavailability sits at approximately 6% per the Geref product label, which is expected for GHRH analogs and still produces reliable pharmacological GH pulses. In practice, sermorelin is the "start here" peptide on r/Peptides (roughly 95,000 subscribers). Community dosing runs 200 to 300 mcg nightly, almost always co-injected with ipamorelin for dual-pathway GH release. Sleep improvement within the first two weeks is the most consistently reported early effect across hundreds of threads. Body composition shifts require two to three months of patience. No new large RCTs for anti-aging indications have been published between 2024 and 2026, so the adult off-label evidence base relies on the 1990s clinical data combined with a large, consistent community experience. Compared to CJC-1295 (No DAC), sermorelin has a measured half-life, 11 to 12 minutes on the Geref label. It also has more clinical data and an FDA approval history. Geref Diagnostic was approved in 1990 (therapeutic Geref in 1997), and both were discontinued in 2008, and FDA withdrew its approvals effective June 18, 2009 (74 FR 23407). CJC-1295 has zero completed human trials for anti-aging indications.

Sermorelin binds the growth hormone releasing hormone receptor (GHRH-R) on anterior pituitary somatotroph cells. This is the same receptor that endogenous GHRH activates to trigger natural GH secretion. The 1-29 amino acid fragment retains full receptor binding affinity because the N-terminal portion of GHRH contains all the structural elements needed for GHRH-R recognition and activation. Once GHRH-R activates, it triggers intracellular cyclic AMP signaling in somatotrophs. That cascade opens calcium channels, prompting GH vesicle release into circulation. The resulting GH pulse peaks at approximately 30 to 60 minutes post-injection and clears quickly. The Geref label gives sermorelin a plasma half-life of 11 to 12 minutes after IV or subcutaneous dosing. The short half-life is actually a feature. It produces a discrete pulse rather than sustained tonic GH elevation, preserving the natural pulsatile secretion rhythm. The downstream chain follows a predictable path. Pulsatile GH stimulates hepatic IGF-1 synthesis, and IGF-1 mediates most of the tissue-level effects: protein synthesis, lipolysis, collagen production, and bone metabolism. Because sermorelin works through the pituitary rather than replacing GH directly, the hypothalamic feedback loop stays intact. Somatostatin still is the natural brake on GH secretion. This self-limiting mechanism is why supraphysiological GH levels are uncommon with sermorelin at standard doses. The antibody issue is worth understanding mechanistically. Sermorelin is a foreign peptide analog. Repeated daily injection can trigger an adaptive immune response. The Geref label reports that a large proportion of patients develop anti-GRF antibodies at least once during treatment, often transiently. In the children studied, the antibodies did not appear to affect growth. Cycling cuts total antigen exposure, which is why many protocols build in breaks.
Sermorelin benefits center on GH release through your own pituitary, which community users favor as the conservative route. The largest trial was in GH-deficient children; adult studies are small.

Improved sleep depth and duration within one to two weeks of starting is the most consistently first-reported benefit across hundreds of r/Peptides threads. A placebo-controlled trial in older adults found no change in sleep quality after 16 weeks of a GHRH analog (Khorram et al. 1997) [1].
Skin thickness rose in men and women aged 55 to 71 after 16 weeks of a nightly GHRH analog. Lean mass rose in men only, and fat mass didn't change (Khorram et al. 1997) [1].

Height velocity in GH-deficient children rose from 4.1 to 7.2 cm per year after 12 months on 30 mcg/kg/day (Geref International Study Group) [2]. No adverse biochemical or hormonal changes turned up. A later review [4] cites data in a few children suggesting the effect holds through 36 months.

Preserved pituitary feedback. Unlike exogenous GH, sermorelin works through the GHRH receptor, keeping the somatostatin brake functional and making supraphysiological GH levels unlikely at standard doses.
Better workout recovery by weeks three to four is widely reported in community threads, with reduced muscle soreness and faster bounce-back between training sessions.
Skin hydration and texture improvements at months three and beyond, consistent with GH-driven collagen synthesis.
Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 10 key studies · compounded

Mechanism well-established: sermorelin is the 1–29 N-terminal fragment of endogenous GHRH, fully retaining GHRH receptor (GHRH-R) binding activity and stimulating pulsatile GH release from the pituitary somatotrophs.

Dosing studied: No trial set an adult dose. Older-adult studies used 0.5 or 1 mg GHRH(1-29) SC twice daily for 14 days (PMID 1379256) and 10 mcg/kg of an analog nightly for 16 weeks (PMID 9141536); pediatric 30 mcg/kg/day SC (PMID 8772599)

FDA-approved 1990 and 1997 (Geref) for GH deficiency diagnosis and pediatric GH deficiency treatment; discontinued by EMD Serono in 2008; FDA found the withdrawal was not for safety or effectiveness reasons, and both approvals were withdrawn in 2009. In GH-deficient children, nightly dosing raised height velocity in an open-label study [2]. A randomized trial of 60 GH-deficient children compared GH with a GHRH(1-29)-NH2 infusion [5]. GH grew them faster: 14.6 vs about 9.2 cm/yr at 6 months. Khorram et al. 1997 [1] gave 19 adults aged 55 to 71 a nightly [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) analog for 16 weeks. IGF-1 rose early but drifted back toward baseline by week 16; skin thickness rose, lean mass rose in men only, and sleep quality didn't change. The Geref label reports that a large proportion of patients develop anti-GRF antibodies at least once during treatment, often transiently. In the children studied, the antibodies did not appear to affect growth. No new large RCTs published 2024–2026 for anti-aging off-label indications.
Key Study

Khorram et al. 1997 (PMID 9141536): nightly SC [Nle27]GHRH(1-29)-NH2 for 16 weeks in 19 adults aged 55 to 71. IGF-1 up by week 2, back toward baseline by week 16; skin thickness up, lean mass up in men only, sleep quality unchanged. Geref International Study Group (PMID 8772599): 30 mcg/kg/day SC in 110 GH-deficient children (86 analyzed). Height velocity 4.1 to 7.2 cm/yr at 12 months.
Limitations

The adult studies are small. Khorram 1997 gave 19 adults aged 55 to 71 an analog for 16 weeks (PMID 9141536). Corpas 1992 gave 10 older men GHRH(1-29) for 14 days (PMID 1379256). The largest trial was in 110 GH-deficient children (PMID 8772599). No large modern RCT has tested adult anti-aging or body composition use. Off-label dosing (200–500 mcg adult) is community-derived, not established by an RCT. Antibody formation data from the original Geref label (pre-2008): long-term antibody impact in current compounded formulations not re-studied. SC bioavailability ~6% (expected for GHRH analogs).
Community Experience
Widely regarded as the most conservative, beginner-appropriate GH secretagogue.
Community dosing: 200–300 mcg SC nightly most often, up to 500 mcg in some protocols; typically co-injected with ipamorelin 200 mcg; 5 days on / 2 days off

"Start here before CJC/Ipa" is the dominant consensus. Primary uses: sleep optimization, anti-aging, modest body recomposition. Nearly always stacked with ipamorelin to pair a GHRH signal with a GHRP pulse.
What users report (5)
Improved sleep depth and duration: most consistent first-reported benefit (weeks 1–2)
Better workout recovery and reduced soreness by weeks 3–4
Gradual fat loss and improved muscle tone over months 2–3
Improved skin hydration and quality at months 3+
Well-tolerated: low side-effect burden relative to synthetic GH
Common issues (5)
Slow onset: visible body composition changes require 2–3 months; common expectation mismatch
Efficacy plateau or loss after 4–6 months in continuous non-cycled users (antibody formation)
Strict pre-injection fasting required (2+ hours): compliance is the most common failure point
Facial flushing and mild headache common in first 1–3 weeks post-injection
Results modest vs. CJC-1295/ipamorelin stack: some users switch after first cycle
Science & Community Aligned

Science and community agree on GHRH-R mechanism, pulsatile GH release, and SC nightly dosing. Community doses (200–500 mcg nightly) sit below the doses older-adult studies used (10 mcg/kg nightly, PMID 9141536; 1 mg twice daily, PMID 1379256). Bedtime administration, empty stomach requirement, and 5-day cycling are all mechanistically grounded in published pharmacology. Primary divergence: community almost always stacks sermorelin with ipamorelin while clinical trials tested sermorelin monotherapy. Antibody formation concern is present in both clinical data and community experience.
Community Compounded sermorelin: community dosing reports (200 to 300 mcg most often, up to 500 mcg); no adult trial set a dose

With a 5 mg vial and 2 mL bacteriostatic water, you get 2,500 mcg/mL. At that concentration: 200 mcg is 8 units on a U-100 insulin syringe, 300 mcg is 12 units, and 500 mcg is 20 units. The fasting window is where most beginners fail. You need at least two hours with no food before the injection. Insulin triggers somatostatin release from the hypothalamus, which directly opposes GH secretion. Eating within that window doesn't just reduce the effect; it negates it. Bedtime dosing is the priority. Sermorelin amplifies the natural nocturnal GH pulse during slow-wave sleep. Inject 30 to 60 minutes before sleep for best results. Store reconstituted vials at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius. Discard anything cloudy or with visible particles. Lyophilized powder is more stable but still belongs in the fridge. If you see no sleep improvement after two weeks with correct timing, check your reconstitution math first. Then get an IGF-1 draw at week six. If IGF-1 isn't moving, suspect the product quality before blaming the peptide. Most users stack sermorelin with ipamorelin. The two hit different receptor pathways (GHRH-R and GHS-R1a), and community reports describe a combined GH pulse larger than either alone.
Sermorelin Cycle

The Geref label reports that a large proportion of patients develop anti-GRF antibodies at least once during treatment, often transiently. In the children studied, the antibodies did not appear to affect growth. Their effect on results in adults is not studied. The antibody response is driven by repeated antigen exposure. Cycling (5-days-on/2-days-off and periodic 4-week breaks) reduces total antigen exposure, mitigates immune sensitization, and helps maintain long-term pituitary responsiveness.
Declining sleep quality improvement despite consistent dosing (months 4–6)
IGF-1 levels plateauing or declining after initial elevation on the same dose
Loss of recovery and energy benefits previously present on the same protocol
Reduced or absent facial flushing post-injection (may indicate diminished GH pulse response)

Calculate your syringe units At 2,500 mcg/mL (5 mg vial + 2 mL BAC water): 200 mcg = 8 units, 300 mcg = 12 units, 500 mcg = 20 units on a U-100 insulin syringe.
Confirm fasting Minimum two hours since your last meal. No food for 30 minutes after injection, either.
Clean the injection site with an alcohol swab Abdomen (periumbilical area, avoiding the navel) or lateral thigh. Rotate sides with each injection.
Pinch the skin at the injection site Insert the needle at a 45-degree angle. Inject slowly and hold for five seconds before withdrawing. Use a 27 to 31 gauge, 5/16 inch or 3/8 inch needle.

If stacking with ipamorelin, draw sermorelin first, then ipamorelin into the same syringe. Co-inject at the same site and time. For a typical beginner stack: 8 units sermorelin (200 mcg from a 5 mg/2 mL vial) plus 20 units ipamorelin (200 mcg from a 2 mg/2 mL vial).
Inject 30 to 60 minutes before sleep Store the reconstituted vial in the refrigerator immediately after use.
Cycling: 5 days on, 2 days off (for example, Monday through Friday). Take a full four-week break after each three-to-six-month cycle to prevent antibody formation.
Alternative Routes
Subcutaneous injection
Reference route; all published dosing data based on SC administration

SC bioavailability ~6% (Geref label). Despite low absolute bioavailability, SC reliably produces pharmacological GH pulses. Inject into abdomen (periumbilical) or lateral thigh fat, rotating sites. 27–31G 5/16" or 3/8" insulin needle standard.
Sublingual tablet
Bioavailability unknown: no PK study comparing sublingual vs. SC sermorelin published as of April 2026. Tablets marketed at $79–$139/month; dose equivalence to SC injection unestablished.

Sublingual sermorelin tablets are now available through some telehealth platforms. Sermorelin is a 29-amino-acid peptide: sublingual absorption of intact peptides is generally low due to protease activity and mucosal impermeability. Patients should understand this is an unvalidated route with no comparative efficacy data vs. the clinically established SC route.
Intranasal
Intranasal bioavailability for GHRH analogs estimated ~20% of SC in limited studies; sermorelin-specific intranasal PK data not published

Not a standard clinical or commercial route for sermorelin. Some compounding pharmacies have prepared intranasal formulations but this is not supported by published efficacy data for sermorelin specifically.
Works With
Ipamorelin

The most common community pairing. Ipamorelin acts on GHS-R1a, a different receptor from sermorelin's GHRH-R, and community reports describe a larger GH pulse from the pair than from either alone. In swine, ipamorelin released GH without raising ACTH or cortisol (PMID 9849822).
200 mcg sermorelin + 200 mcg ipamorelin co-injected SC, 30–60 min before sleep
BPC-157
Added for systemic recovery, gut health, and injury healing while sermorelin handles GH optimization. No direct pharmacokinetic interaction. Injected separately at a different site and timing.
BPC-157 250–500 mcg SC separate injection, separate site; timing flexible
TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4)

Added to sermorelin protocols for enhanced tissue repair and anti-inflammatory effects, particularly in athletes. GH optimization (sermorelin) + systemic healing (TB-500) is a popular body recomposition stack.
TB-500 2–5 mg SC 1–2× per week; separate injection from sermorelin
Avoid
Tesamorelin

Both are GHRH-R agonists: concurrent use is redundant and provides receptor competition without additive benefit. Tesamorelin is significantly more potent; combining does not amplify effect. Choose one GHRH analog per cycle.
CJC-1295 (with DAC)

CJC-1295 DAC produces a prolonged continuous GHRH signal (t½ ~7 days) that is mechanistically incompatible with sermorelin's pulsatile GHRH approach. The DAC formulation blunts GH pulsatility that sermorelin is designed to optimize. Concurrent use is counterproductive and redundant.
Glucocorticoids (prednisone, dexamethasone, chronic use)

Chronic glucocorticoid use blunts pituitary GH secretion and reduces the IGF-1 response to sermorelin. Documented in the Geref prescribing information as a drug interaction. Short-course steroids have minimal impact; chronic use substantially reduces sermorelin efficacy.
Somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide)
Somatostatin analogs directly suppress GH release from pituitary somatotrophs: pharmacologically opposing sermorelin's mechanism. Concurrent use eliminates sermorelin efficacy.

Antibody formation is the main long-term question with sermorelin. The Geref label reports that a large proportion of patients develop anti-GRF antibodies at least once during treatment, often transiently. In the children studied, the antibodies did not appear to affect growth. The label also links them to no specific adverse reaction profile. Users who skip cycling and run sermorelin continuously for six-plus months commonly report complete loss of effect. Community protocols respond by cutting injection frequency (5 days on, 2 days off) and taking periodic four-week breaks. Facial flushing is the most common acute side effect. It typically occurs 20 to 30 minutes after injection and results from the vasodilatory response to acute GH release. Community reports and clinical data both describe this as transient, resolving within an hour, and most prominent during the first one to three weeks of use. It does not require dose adjustment unless severe. Headache and dizziness post-injection are reported at moderate frequency. Like flushing, these relate to the acute GH pulse. They tend to resolve by weeks three to four without intervention. If persistent, reducing the dose by 50 mcg usually handles it. Injection-site reactions (redness, minor irritation, occasional nodules) are expected with any subcutaneous peptide. Consistent site rotation and allowing refrigerated peptide to reach room temperature before injecting both reduce incidence. Nodules persisting beyond one week warrant switching to a different anatomical region. GH-mediated insulin resistance is a theoretical concern with any GH-raising therapy. Sermorelin produces physiological (not supraphysiological) GH pulses, so the risk is lower than with exogenous GH. Still, fasting glucose monitoring every three months is appropriate, especially for anyone over 40 or carrying metabolic risk factors. A fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL means stopping. GH promotes cell proliferation. Active cancer, a history of malignancy, or active pituitary tumors are absolute contraindications. If IGF-1 surpasses the age-adjusted upper normal range, the dose should be reduced or the protocol discontinued. Untreated hypothyroidism impairs GH response to sermorelin (Geref contraindications). GH also accelerates T4-to-T3 conversion, so thyroid function may shift during use. Baseline thyroid panel is recommended. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are contraindicated. Effects on fetal development have not been established. When to see a doctor: persistent edema, fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL, joint pain unresponsive to dose reduction, symptoms of intracranial hypertension, or any sign of glucose intolerance.
Common Issues & Solutions

No sleep improvement after 2 weeks → verify timing (30–60 min pre-sleep, ≥2 hours fasted); confirm reconstitution math (5 mg + 2 mL BAC water = 2,500 mcg/mL; 200 mcg = 8 units); confirm vial is refrigerated at 2–8°C and solution is clear.

Efficacy plateau or loss after 4–6 months → antibody formation is one suspect, though on the Geref label antibodies were often transient and did not appear to affect growth in the children studied; implement strict 5-on/2-off cycling if not already doing so; schedule a 4-week complete break; efficacy typically returns post-break.

IGF-1 not rising after 6–8 weeks at 200 mcg → dose may be subtherapeutic; titrate to 300 mcg; rule out concurrent hypothyroidism (check TSH/T3/T4), chronic glucocorticoid use, or injection technique error (IM vs. SC).

Facial flushing, headache, or dizziness post-injection → benign vasodilatory response to GH release; typically resolves by weeks 3–4 without dose change; if severe or persistent, reduce dose by 50 mcg; does not require discontinuation.

Injection site nodules or persistent irritation → rotate sites consistently (alternating abdominal sides, lateral thighs); allow refrigerated peptide to reach room temperature before injecting; confirm SC technique (not IM depth); switch anatomical region if nodules persist >1 week.

Sermorelin: Product Quality medium risk

Sermorelin was the active ingredient of an FDA-approved drug (Geref), and US clinics prescribe it compounded rather than as a research chemical. As a compounded (not FDA-manufactured) product, GMP compliance, sterility, and potency are pharmacy-dependent and unverified by FDA. Grey-market research chemical vials exist and carry substantially higher contamination and misdosing risk.
Source exclusively from licensed 503A compounding pharmacies with a valid clinician prescription
A certificate of analysis (COA) or potency/sterility report documents a compounded batch; licensed 503A compounders can provide one
Verify reconstitution math independently: 5 mg vial + 2 mL BAC water = 2,500 mcg/mL; 200 mcg = 8 units on a U-100 insulin syringe
Refrigerate reconstituted vials at 2–8°C; discard if solution is cloudy, discolored, or contains visible particulates
Research-chemical products without an independent third-party COA carry real risk: underdosing and contamination are documented in the grey market

FDA approved sermorelin acetate as Geref in 1990 (NDA 019863), a diagnostic for pituitary GH secretion. A second Geref approval in 1997 (NDA 020443) covered idiopathic GH deficiency in children with growth failure. Geref was discontinued by EMD Serono in 2008; FDA found the withdrawal was not for safety or effectiveness reasons (78 FR 14095). FDA withdrew both approvals effective June 18, 2009 (74 FR 23407), so no FDA-approved sermorelin product exists in the US today. Sermorelin is not on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) or on FDA's list of drugs withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons (21 CFR 216.24). FDA's 503B list (updated March 21, 2025) places sermorelin acetate in Category 1, under evaluation, and marks it as a component of an FDA-approved drug. US clinics prescribe compounded sermorelin; no compounded product has FDA approval. Some telehealth services offer sublingual tablets, and no published pharmacokinetic study compares sublingual to subcutaneous dosing. Athletes should know that sermorelin falls under the WADA 2026 Prohibited List as a Growth Hormone Releasing Factor (S2.2.4). It is detectable and any athlete subject to anti-doping testing should not use it. This content is for educational and research purposes only. Nothing here constitutes medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any peptide.

phases.notes: Continue through month 6. Repeat IGF-1 at months 3 and 6. If IGF-1 surpasses upper-normal or side effects emerge, reduce to 200 mcg. Take a 4-week complete break before restarting.

protocols.monitoringNotes: IGF-1 baseline, week 6, month 3, month 6. Fasting glucose baseline and every 3 months. Thyroid panel at baseline (hypothyroidism blunts GH response).

protocols.goal: GH optimization: sermorelin + ipamorelin dual-pathway stack

phases.name: Induction
phases.syringeUnits: Draw 8 units sermorelin (5 mg/2 mL vial = 2,500 mcg/mL), then 20 units ipamorelin (2 mg/2 mL vial = 1,000 mcg/mL) into same insulin syringe before injecting
phases.timing: 30–60 min before sleep; minimum 2 hours fasted
phases.notes: Community reports describe a larger GH pulse from GHRH (sermorelin) + GHRP (ipamorelin) than from either alone, via complementary receptor pathways (GHRH-R + GHS-R1a). Draw sermorelin first, then ipamorelin into the same syringe.

phases.name: Steady state
phases.frequency: Once daily (bedtime), 5 days on / 2 days off
phases.syringeUnits: 8–12 units sermorelin + 20 units ipamorelin (2 mg/2 mL = 1,000 mcg/mL): co-injected
phases.timing: 30–60 min before sleep; minimum 2 hours fasted
phases.notes: Check IGF-1 at week 6. Titrate sermorelin dose to achieve IGF-1 in mid-normal range for age. Ipamorelin held at 200 mcg (dose ceiling for GH selectivity). 5-on/2-off cycling minimum.

protocols.duration: 3–4 months per cycle; 4-week break before restarting
protocols.monitoringNotes: IGF-1 at baseline, week 6, month 3. Fasting glucose baseline and monthly. Monitor for edema and joint discomfort (GH-mediated).

protocols.goal: GH optimization: higher-dose, IGF-1 guided (clinician supervised)

phases.name: Baseline establishment
phases.syringeUnits: 12 units (5 mg vial + 2 mL BAC water = 2,500 mcg/mL)
phases.timing: 30–60 min before sleep; minimum 2–3 hours fasted
phases.notes: Full baseline labs required: IGF-1, fasting glucose, HbA1c, thyroid panel (T3/T4/TSH), CBC. Physician supervision required at this dosing tier.

phases.name: Titration to target IGF-1
phases.frequency: Once daily (bedtime), 5 days on / 2 days off
phases.syringeUnits: 12 units at 300 mcg; 20 units at 500 mcg (5 mg vial + 2 mL BAC water = 2,500 mcg/mL)
phases.timing: 30–60 min before sleep; minimum 2–3 hours fasted
phases.notes: Titrate in 50–100 mcg increments at 4-week intervals. Target mid-normal IGF-1 for age/sex. Do not exceed 500 mcg/day without physician oversight. Repeat IGF-1 every 4 weeks during titration.

phases.name: Maintenance at target dose
phases.frequency: Once daily (bedtime), 5 days on / 2 days off
phases.syringeUnits: 12–20 units depending on target dose (5 mg vial + 2 mL BAC water = 2,500 mcg/mL)
phases.timing: 30–60 min before sleep; minimum 2–3 hours fasted
phases.notes: Maintain dose that keeps IGF-1 in mid-normal range. Repeat labs at month 3 and month 6. After 6 months, take a 4-week break; if IGF-1 response is diminished on restart, antibody formation is likely.

protocols.duration: 6 months; 4-week break; assess antibody effect before repeat cycle
protocols.monitoringNotes: IGF-1 every 4 weeks during titration, then every 3 months. Fasting glucose and HbA1c baseline and every 3 months. Thyroid panel at baseline. Optional DEXA at 6 months.

faqs.q: What is the recommended sermorelin dosage?
faqs.a: Community protocols start at 200 mcg subcutaneous before bed and most often stay at 200 to 300 mcg; some go to 500 mcg. No adult trial set a dose. Studies in older adults used 10 mcg/kg of an analog nightly (PMID 9141536) or 1 mg twice daily for 14 days in 10 men (PMID 1379256). Bedtime dosing lines up with the natural GH pulse in deep sleep, and many protocols run 5 days on and 2 days off.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of sermorelin?
faqs.a: Injection site reactions (redness, swelling) are the most common. Facial flushing post-injection occurs in about 15-20% of users and usually fades after 2-3 weeks. Headache and dizziness are less common. The Geref label reports that a large proportion of patients develop anti-GRF antibodies at least once during treatment, often transiently. In the children studied, the antibodies did not appear to affect growth.

faqs.q: How does sermorelin compare to ipamorelin?
faqs.a: Sermorelin is a GHRH analog (binds the GHRH receptor). Ipamorelin is a ghrelin mimetic (binds GHS-R1a). Different receptors, different mechanisms. Community reports describe a larger GH pulse from combining both than from either alone. Sermorelin has more clinical data. Its Geref label also reports that a large proportion of patients develop anti-GRF antibodies, often transiently.

faqs.q: How long does sermorelin take to work?
faqs.a: Sleep quality improvements typically appear within 1-2 weeks. Recovery and energy benefits emerge around weeks 4-6. Body composition changes require 3-6 months of consistent dosing. Antibodies are common on the Geref label; their effect on results in adults is not studied.

No FDA-approved sermorelin product exists today. FDA approved sermorelin acetate as Geref in 1990 and 1997, for diagnosing GH deficiency and for treating it in children. Geref was discontinued by EMD Serono in 2008; FDA found the withdrawal was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. FDA withdrew both approvals effective June 18, 2009 (74 FR 23407). Sermorelin remains available through compounding pharmacies with a prescription, and compounded sermorelin is not an FDA-approved product.
Sermorelin typically comes in 5mg vials. Add 2mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Sermorelin?
faqs.a: The half-life of Sermorelin is 11-12 min (IV or SC, Geref label). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: FDA-approved as Geref in 1990, then discontinued by EMD Serono in 2008; FDA found the withdrawal was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. The sermorelin peptide (Geref) is the first 29 amino acids of endogenous growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH), the biologically active fragment that fully retains pituitary GHRH receptor binding.
